assessment:
This study by Peukes, Lovatt, and colleagues represents a significant technical and conceptual advance in understanding the molecular architecture of glutamatergic synapses in the adult mammalian brain. The authors developed an 'ultra-fresh' sample preparation workflow that combines mouse genetic labeling (Psd95-GFP knockin mice) with cryogenic correlated light and electron microscopy (cryoCLEM) and cryo-electron tomography (cryoET) to visualize synapses within 2 minutes of tissue extraction. This rapid workflow, along with complementary in-tissue imaging of vitreous cryo-sections, aimed to preserve near-physiological molecular architecture while avoiding artifacts associated with conventional electron microscopy preparation methods.

The central and most provocative finding is that the postsynaptic density (PSD)—long considered a defining ultrastructural feature of glutamatergic synapses based on decades of conventional EM studies—is not a conserved feature in native synapses imaged by cryoET. Instead of a consistently higher protein density at the postsynaptic membrane, the authors observed substantial variability: only about half of ultra-fresh synapses and less than half of in-tissue synapses showed increased molecular crowding proximal to the postsynaptic membrane. Control experiments using conventional EM on the same samples consistently revealed PSDs, leading the authors to conclude that the PSD appearance is an artifact of chemical fixation, dehydration, and heavy metal staining. The study also provides detailed characterization of synaptic components including cytoskeletal elements (F-actin networks in all postsynaptic compartments, microtubules in 15% of presynaptic compartments), organelles (mitochondria with calcium phosphate aggregates), membrane remodeling intermediates, and ionotropic glutamate receptors organized in clusters of up to 60 receptors. Notably, 60% of synapses contained receptor clusters partly or completely outside the synaptic cleft, and the synaptic cleft height averaged 33 nm—65% greater than conventional EM measurements but consistent with super-resolution microscopy.

The evidence supporting the main conclusions is generally strong, with multiple complementary approaches (ultra-fresh isolated synapses and anatomically intact tissue sections) yielding consistent results. The rapid sample preparation demonstrably preserves labile structures like microtubules that depolymerize within 1-3 minutes, providing confidence in the near-physiological state of the samples. The molecular density analysis was carefully conducted to avoid projection artifacts, with individual tomographic slices aligned before averaging. The subtomogram averaging of ionotropic glutamate receptors at 25 Å resolution, with good fit to AMPA receptor atomic structures, validates receptor identification. The dataset is substantial (93 ultra-fresh and 50 in-tissue synapse tomograms from multiple mice) with unbiased data collection guided by Psd95-GFP fluorescence. However, some limitations warrant consideration. The ultra-fresh preparation, while rapid, still involves mechanical disruption of tissue and exposure to non-physiological conditions (ice-cold ACSF, homogenization), though the authors argue that preservation of cytoskeletal elements indicates minimal deterioration. The interpretation that the PSD is entirely artifactual is compelling but somewhat speculative—the proposed mechanisms (preferential staining, crosslinking, protein extraction) are plausible but not directly tested. The variability in molecular crowding could alternatively reflect genuine heterogeneity in synaptic states or subtypes, though the authors acknowledge this possibility. The resolution of the tomograms (binned to ~12 Å voxels for analysis) limits identification of specific protein complexes beyond receptors.

This work has important implications for the field of synaptic neuroscience by challenging a foundational concept and demonstrating that native synaptic architecture is more variable and dynamic than previously appreciated. The findings align with emerging views from super-resolution microscopy showing nanoscale organization of synaptic proteins rather than uniform densities. The study also highlights the critical importance of sample preparation methods in structural biology and suggests that many previous interpretations of synaptic ultrastructure may need revision. The technical advances—particularly the integration of genetic labeling with rapid cryopreservation and cryoET—establish a powerful approach for studying native tissue architecture that should be applicable to other biological systems. While some aspects of the interpretation remain open to further investigation, the rigorous methodology, comprehensive dataset, and consistency across multiple experimental approaches provide strong support for the main conclusions.
